# Jennifer L. Wall, PhD

## *Interdisciplinary Postdoctoral Ecologist*

## National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, Smithsonian Institution & Duke Farms, a Center for the Doris Duke Foundation

<br>

I am a wildlife biologist broadly interested in population and community ecology, theoretical and applied modeling, and behavioral ecology. More specifically, I am interested in better understanding how climate and other anthropogenic changes impact species interactions and behavior at the intersection of both applied and theoretical ecology.

I have about 10 years of research experience on a variety of taxa and systems, including planning and implementing a multi-year, collaborative research project assessing the impacts of climate and landcover changes on at-risk wildlife in Alaska. Prior to my current role, I served as a Postdoctoral Research Fellow with [Black Rock Forest](https://www.blackrockforest.org/) and the [Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory](https://lamont.columbia.edu/), where I am built on existing research efforts to understand mammal composition and landscape use in the Hudson Valley, including work on bobcat connectivity and white-tailed deer behavior. I am currently working as a Interdisciplinary Postdoctoral Ecologist with the Smithsonian Institution's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute and Duke Farms, a center for the Doris Duke Foundation, where I am leveraging my research and modeling background to advance regional connectivity efforts in the Northeastern United States.

# Recent Updates

November 2026

  : I presented my work on bobcat functional connectivity modeling at the annual Wildlife Society conference in Des Moinse, Iowa.


October 2026

  : Just published on of my dissertation chapters in *Ecology*, titled, "From peaks to patches: Hierarchical climate filtering in collared pikas and hoary marmots." [See the published manuscript here.](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecy.70503)


September 2026

  : I presented my work on mammalian roadkill hotspots and culvert underpassage usage at the Northeastern Transportation and Wildlife Conference in State college, PA.
  
  : I also transitioned to a new position with the Smithsonian Institution and Duke Farms as an Interdisciplinary Postdoctoral Ecologist!


June 2026

  : Just published one of my dissertation chapters! We found that collared pikas adjusted their activity levels with surface temperatures (not subsurface), were more active at cooler patches with more vegetation, and were not active at all at surface temperatures above 21$^{o}$C. [See the published manuscript here.](https://doi.org/10.1002/oik.11677)

  : I attended the 106th American Society of Mammalogists meeting June 12 -1 15th. [See here for my poster on quantifying significant animal behavior change points](https://www.jlwallphd.com/ASM_2026).  


February 2026
 
  : Caught our first bobcat of the season - welcome, LYRU0008!


January 2026
 
  : Check out our article on bobcat movement ecology in [Black Rock Forest's 2026 Winter newsletter](https://www.blackrockforest.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/2026_winter_newsletter_web.pdf) (Page 2).
